plain_english:
My dear Serenus, I think Athenodorus gave up too easily. He retreated too quickly from public life. I won't deny that sometimes you need to step back. But you should retreat slowly, with dignity. Keep your standards high and your honor intact. Soldiers who negotiate while still holding their weapons get more respect from their enemies. They're also safer.

This is what virtue should do. This is what anyone trying to live well should do. If Fortune gets the upper hand and blocks your ability to act, don't immediately turn and run. Don't throw down your weapons and hide. There's no place Fortune can't find you anyway. Instead, be more careful about taking on public roles. Think it through. Find some way you can still serve your country.
original_excerpt: To me, my dearest Serenus, Athenodorus seems to have yielded too completely to the times, to have fled too soon: I will not deny that sometimes one must retire, but one ought to retire slowly, at a foot’s pace, without losing one’s ensigns or one’s honour as a soldier: those who make terms with arms in their hands are more respected by their enemies and more safe in their hands. This is what I think ought to be done by virtue and by one who practises virtue: if Fortune get the upper hand and deprive him of the power of action, let him not straightway turn his back to the enemy, throw away his arms, and run away seeking for a hiding-place, as if there were any place whither Fortune could not pursue him, but let him be more sparing in his acceptance of public office, and after due deliberation discover some means by which he can be of use to the state. He is not able to serve in the army: then let him become a candidate for civic honours: must he live in a private station?

plain_english: Can't serve in the army? Then run for public office. Must live as a private citizen? Then become a lawyer. Are you forced to stay silent? Then help your fellow citizens with quiet advice. Is it dangerous to even enter the public square? Then be a good companion, a loyal friend, a well-behaved guest in homes, at public events, and at parties. Have you lost your citizenship? Then act like a human being. We proudly refuse to limit ourselves to one city. We go out to connect with all lands and call ourselves citizens of the world. Why? So we have a bigger stage to show our virtue.
original_excerpt: then let him be an advocate: is he condemned to keep silence? then let him help his countrymen with silent counsel. Is it dangerous for him even to enter the forum? then let him prove himself a good comrade, a faithful friend, a sober guest in people’s houses, at public shows, and at wine-parties. Suppose that he has lost the status of a citizen; then let him exercise that of a man: our reason for magnanimously refusing to confine ourselves within the walls of one city, for having gone forth to enjoy intercourse with all lands and for professing ourselves to be citizens of the world is that we may thus obtain a wider theatre on which to display our virtue. Is the bench of judges closed to you, are you forbidden to address the people from the hustings, or to be a candidate at elections? then turn your eyes away from Rome, and see what a wide extent of territory, what a number of nations present themselves before you.

plain_english:
Are you banned from being a judge? Can't you speak to the people or run for office? Then look beyond Rome. See how much territory there is, how many nations stretch before you. It's impossible for every door to your ambitions to be shut — there are always more paths open. But ask yourself: is this ban really your own fault?

You refuse to serve the state unless you can be consul or some other high official. What if someone refused to serve in the army unless they could be a general or officer? Even if others form the front line and fate puts you with the veterans in back, do your duty there. Use your voice, give encouragement, set an example, show your spirit. Even a man with his hands cut off can help his side in battle if he stands firm and cheers on his comrades.
original_excerpt: Thus, it is never possible for so many outlets to be closed against your ambition that more will not remain open to it: but see whether the whole prohibition does not arise from your own fault. You do not choose to direct the affairs of the state except as consul or prytanis[2] or meddix[3] or sufes:[4] what should we say if you refused to serve in the army save as general or military tribune? Even though others may form the first line, and your lot may have placed you among the veterans of the third, do your duty there with your voice, encouragement, example, and spirit: even though a man’s hands be cut off, he may find means to help his side in a battle, if he stands his ground and cheers on his comrades. Do something of that sort yourself: if Fortune removes you from the front rank, stand your ground nevertheless and cheer on your comrades, and if somebody stops your mouth, stand nevertheless and help your side in silence.

plain_english: Do something like that yourself. If fortune pushes you out of the spotlight, hold your ground anyway and cheer on your teammates. If someone silences you, still stand there and help your side quietly. The work of a good citizen is never wasted. He helps just by being heard and seen — through his face, his gestures, his quiet strength, even the way he walks. Some medicines help us through their smell as well as their taste and touch. Virtue works the same way. Even when it's hidden or far away, it spreads usefulness around. Whether virtue moves freely and enjoys its proper place, or has to appear carefully and pull back during storms, whether it sits unused and silent in tight quarters, or shows itself openly — whatever form it takes, it always does good. Do you really think there's no value in someone who knows how to rest with dignity? The best plan is to mix rest with work. When obstacles or public troubles prevent you from living an active life, you're never so cut off that there's no room left for honorable action.
original_excerpt: The services of a good citizen are never thrown away: he does good by being heard and seen, by his expression, his gestures, his silent determination, and his very walk. As some remedies benefit us by their smell as well as by their their taste and touch, so virtue even when concealed and at a distance sheds usefulness around. Whether she moves at her ease and enjoys her just rights, or can only appear abroad on sufferance and is forced to shorten sail to the tempest, whether it be unemployed, silent, and pent up in a narrow lodging, or openly displayed, in whatever guise she may appear, she always does good. What? do you think that the example of one who can rest nobly has no value? It is by far the best plan, therefore, to mingle leisure with business, whenever chance impediments or the state of public affairs forbid one’s leading an active life: for one is never so cut off from all pursuits as to find no room left for honourable action.
